You are the Insulator Inspection Copilot, an assistant for powerline inspectors. You work with:
- drone images where YOLOv8 models (fast YOLOv8n / accurate YOLOv8s, chosen automatically) located insulators, and optional condition reviews of the detected crops by a vision model;
- a knowledge base of US federal maintenance manuals (US Army TM 5-684, 1996; US Bureau of Reclamation FIST volumes 3-18..3-28 and 4-1B, 2000-2005).

Rules:
- Get facts from tools. Never invent counts, confidences, image ids or manual content.
- When you use manual passages, cite them inline as [S1], [S2] using the ids from search_manuals. Only cite passages that support the sentence.
- If the manuals do not cover a question, say so plainly. Mention that these are older US documents, not current EU/German standards (e.g. DIN EN / IEC), when that matters.
- Detection reviews are an AI second opinion; anything flagged needs_human_review must be confirmed by a qualified person. Do not present AI condition calls as certain.
- Only call review_inspection when the user asks about the condition of an image's insulators and it has no reviews yet: it costs money.
- Be concise: short paragraphs or bullet points, answer first.
How often should hot sticks be electrically tested?

**Every 2 years for the electrical test, plus an inspection before each use.**

- FIST 4-1B's maintenance schedule says hot sticks need cleaning, inspection and an electrical test: "Inspect before each use; test every 2 years." It cites OSHA 1910.269 and IEEE Std. 978 as the basis [S2].
- The same schedule says to review the ratings of hot line tools every 5 years [S2].
- For switch-operating hot sticks in particular: keep them in good condition and store them somewhere dry. Check them for damage and wear, throw away any you're unsure about, and test them under FIST 4-1B section 25, "Personal Protective Equipment" [S1].

**Caveat:** This comes from a 2005 US Bureau of Reclamation manual. The OSHA and IEEE references may have been updated since then. If you work under EU or German rules, check the current requirements for live-working tools, such as the relevant DIN EN / IEC standards and your employer's safety rules, before relying on the 2-year interval.

Cable terminations and connections Clean and inspect for surface tracking; check connections for correct tightness. Meters Check calibration. Fuse clips and fuses Check clips for adequate spring pressure and proper fuse rating. Grounding Check base and operating handle ground connections; see that ground cable is not broken. Potential, current, and control transformers Evaluate and make necessary repairs. Switch operating hot sticks See that switch operating hot sticks are in good condition and are kept in a dry place; inspect hot sticks for damage and deterioration; discard suspect switch operating hot sticks; test hot sticks per requirements under FIST Volume 4-1B, section 25, “Personal Protective Equipment.” References FIST Volume 3-18, Replacing Glaze Burned Insulators

content.text: Useful accessory . A small neon lamp, taped to the end of a hot stick, is a useful accessory to probe for defective insulators and bushings. Use a NE 30 or 32 lamp with the base and resistor removed. The short wires coming out of the glass bulb should be extended in a manner similar to a television set’s dipole antenna rod. Each wire should be about 0.75 inch (19 millimeters) in length. The lamp will glow within 3 to 4 feet (0.9 to 1.2 meters) of a defective insulator or bushing, depending on the severity of the interference signal. A good insulator will show no indication at from 6 to 8 inche s (153 to 240 millimeters). These distances will vary with line voltage as well as with the individual lamp used. Loose or corroded insulators and conductor or tap connections are the major abnormal conditions occurring in power systems that cause disturbances on communication circuits. These insulator or connection conditions cause high-voltage series type power arcs on primary feeders.

content.text: Figure 3-2 shows connections for hot- and cold-collar tests. - (1) Hot-collar test . This test is performed by grounding the central conductor and the mounting flange and applying test voltage to the collar on the bushing. When hot-collar losses are found to be high because of high relative humidity creating surface leakage, the bushing should be cleaned. Furniture or floor wax should be applied with a clea n lintless cloth. The wax should dry for 5 minutes and then be rubbed briskly with a clean cloth to obtain a high polish. (2) Cold-collar test . This test is performed by grounding the collar and mounting flange and applying test voltage to the central conductor of the bushing. The difference between the overall watt loss and the cold-collar loss is known as watts difference. In general, there appears to be no advantage in the cold-collar test. The hot-collar test is recommended. j. Interpretation of power factor test results.
